## Ahu Hanga Poukura: an unrestored moai platform on Rapa Nui

Ahu Hanga Poukura stands on the southern coast of [Easter Island](/chile/place/easter-island/), known to its people as Rapa Nui. The remains of a ceremonial stone platform survive here, with fallen moai statues nearby. Ocean, short grass, and dark volcanic rocks form a landscape in which the monument can be seen without the modern reconstruction of an upright row of figures.

Unlike the island's famous restored complexes, Hanga Poukura offers a sense of how time has left its archaeological heritage. To understand the site, it is more useful to examine the platform, the positions of the statues, and the surrounding terrain than to look for the familiar row of moai facing inland.

## What is an ahu, and what was its role?

**Ahu** are stone platforms associated with ceremonial life in Rapa Nui communities and the veneration of ancestors. Some platforms supported monumental moai sculptures. The precise design and history of each complex vary from one part of the island to another.

Moai are famous for their large heads, long noses, pronounced brows, and elongated ears. Yet they are full figures with torsos, carved mainly from volcanic tuff. Stone was quarried and worked around [Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/), from where many statues were transported to their platforms.

At Hanga Poukura, the **combination of ruined architecture and fallen sculptures** is especially striking. The fragments do not form a neat museum row, so pay attention to the smaller stone elements as well. They show that an ahu was a carefully designed structure, not merely a base for statues.

## Why are the moai at Hanga Poukura lying down?

On Easter Island today, you can see both restored platforms with upright moai and complexes where the figures remain fallen. The history of the monuments' destruction is complex, involving changes in island communities, the passage of time, natural forces, and different historical events. It would be inaccurate to assign one cause to the position of each statue without archaeological evidence.

Hanga Poukura is one of the sites where the statues **have remained fallen**, making it especially interesting to examine closely. From authorized viewing areas, you can appreciate the scale of the stone bodies, the tuff surfaces, and the platform's components without touching the antiquities.

Restored complexes show how a monument looked when upright. An unrestored platform reveals what fragments remain on the ground and the challenges faced by archaeologists and heritage conservation specialists.

## How to explore Hanga Poukura

Begin with a broad view of the coast and platform. From a little distance, you can see how the structure is positioned in relation to the ocean. Then study individual figures and blocks from permitted viewing points.

Look for several features:

- the shape and length of the stone platform;
- the position of fallen moai relative to its base;
- the statues' material and visible weathering;
- the relationship between the monument, shoreline, and surrounding landscape.

Facial details have survived to different degrees on individual moai. This reflects the nature of the stone and prolonged exposure to natural forces. Strong winds and salty air make coastal sites especially vulnerable, so protecting their surfaces is essential.

For photographs, both a wide ocean view and closer shots of stone fragments can be compelling **from an authorized distance**. Do not climb the platform, move stones, touch the statues, or pass beyond barriers.

## How Hanga Poukura differs from other ahu

The island has several important complexes, each revealing another side of its ancient culture.

| Site | Main distinction |
|---|---|
| Hanga Poukura | Fallen moai |
| [Ahu Akahanga](/chile/place/ahu-akahanga/) | Coastal ruins |
| [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/) | Restored row |
| [Tahai](/chile/place/tahai/) | Oceanfront complex |

Unlike Ahu Akivi, where the statues stand upright, Hanga Poukura presents an unrestored monument. The comparison becomes even more interesting after visiting [Puna Pau Quarry](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/): there you can learn about the stone used for the red headpieces of some moai, while here the focus is the platform and sculptures themselves.

When planning an island itinerary, alternate different types of sites rather than choosing stops simply by the number of statues. [Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/) explains how moai were made, restored ahu show their original placement, and unrestored complexes reveal the condition of the surviving archaeological remains.

## Getting there and allowing enough time

Visitors usually reach Hanga Poukura on guided road excursions around [Rapa Nui](/chile/place/easter-island/). [Hanga Roa](/chile/place/hanga-roa/) is the usual departure point for island trips. Stop order and driving times depend on the itinerary, road conditions, and access rules in force.

Viewing the archaeological remains takes less time than a long hiking route. Still, allow for visits to other ahu, the guide's explanations, and photography. Assigning the same number of minutes to every monument makes little sense: some reward a broad viewpoint, while others call for a detailed account of individual fragments.

**An important distinction:** a site's inclusion in a tour itinerary does not establish that every part can be accessed independently at any time. Check whether the relevant area is open and which viewing route is permitted before traveling.

## Rules for visiting archaeological sites

Rapa Nui National Park protects a substantial part of the island's archaeological heritage. At officially open sites, the park sets access conditions, ticket rules, and guiding requirements. Official advice requires staying on marked paths, respecting site boundaries, not touching moai or ahu, not collecting archaeological objects, and not flying drones without permission.

The specific access status **of Hanga Poukura** and any requirement for an accompanying guide should be confirmed with the local organizer and protected-area administration. A general park ticket should not be interpreted as permission to enter every archaeological site on the island.

The coast can be windy. Bring comfortable shoes with good grip, sun protection, and a light windproof jacket; rock and earth can be slippery in rain.

## Ahu Hanga Poukura in Ada Tours itineraries

We include the monument in our current [Easter Island: three days among moai and volcanoes tour](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/). On the last day, a guided excursion in English visits [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/), Hanga Poukura, [Puna Pau](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/), and [Tahai](/chile/place/tahai/), followed by an airport transfer.

Hanga Poukura also features in [Colorful Santiago and Mysterious Easter Island](/chile/tour/santiago-easter-island/) as an unrestored platform on an island sightseeing excursion. For travelers adding Rapa Nui to a longer South American journey, there is a [grand itinerary through Peru, Bolivia, and Chile](/multi-country/tour/south-america-luxury-33-days/).

In each case, compare the actual days, language of guiding, time allocated to monuments, and included services. The same ahu may appear in trips with very different overall paces.

## Frequently asked questions about Ahu Hanga Poukura

### Are the moai at Hanga Poukura standing or lying down?

They are lying down. This is an unrestored archaeological complex with fallen statues and the remains of a stone platform.

### How is it different from Ahu Akivi?

At [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/), visitors see a restored arrangement of upright moai. Hanga Poukura reveals ruins and statues left on the ground.

### Can visitors approach the moai closely?

Only within designated viewing areas. Touching statues, stepping onto platforms, or moving archaeological fragments is prohibited. Confirm the specific access rules before visiting.

### How much time is needed to see Hanga Poukura?

That depends on the sightseeing route and the guide's explanations. On our current [three-day island tour](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/), the stop forms part of a four-hour excursion visiting several monuments, not a separate four-hour examination of this single ahu.

## Which tours visit Ahu Hanga Poukura?

At [Ahu Hanga Poukura](/chile/place/ahu-hanga-poukura/), visitors see the remains of an ancient platform and fallen stone figures against a rocky coastline. The site is valuable precisely because it has not been fully reconstructed: it helps us imagine how many Rapa Nui ahu looked before the restoration of the best-known complexes.

Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} featuring Ahu Hanga Poukura as a main-route stop. It is especially important to read each day's program. Not every [Easter Island](/chile/place/easter-island/) tour includes Hanga Poukura, even if it visits [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/).

## A short island itinerary: different types of platforms

On the [three-day Easter Island tour](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/), Hanga Poukura is scheduled for day three. The excursion starts with the seven restored moai at Ahu Akivi, continues to the unrestored coastal platform, then visits [Puna Pau Quarry](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/) and [Tahai](/chile/place/tahai/). Four hours are allocated to this outing, followed by an airport transfer.

Seeing these sites together lets travelers compare stone monuments in different conditions. At Ahu Akivi, the figures stand upright; at Hanga Poukura, fallen fragments are visible; and at Puna Pau, you can see the material used for red stone headpieces. The quarries, platforms, and ceremonial spaces played different roles in island community life.

## Santiago or a grand South American journey: comparing trips

[Colorful Santiago and Mysterious Easter Island](/chile/tour/santiago-easter-island/) combines Chile's capital, Valparaíso, Viña del Mar, and island archaeology. The final sightseeing day on Rapa Nui includes Ahu Akivi, unrestored Hanga Poukura, Puna Pau, and Tahai. It is a group excursion with an English-speaking guide. The tour is suited to travelers who want to combine the island with mainland Chile without an extended trip through several countries.

On the [33-day VIP journey through Peru, Bolivia, and Chile](/multi-country/tour/south-america-luxury-33-days/), Hanga Poukura is part of a central Rapa Nui excursion together with Ahu Akivi, Puna Pau, and Tahai. This takes place late in the journey, after a long itinerary through Peru and Bolivia. Travelers choose this option for South America as a whole; the archaeological stop is just one part of a substantial multi-country route.

If your principal aim is to see several island monuments, the short [three-day program](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/) minimizes long transfers. If cities and other countries matter too, consider flights, changes of region, and the number of days spent on Rapa Nui.

## Why Hanga Poukura is not a substitute for Tongariki

[Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/), with its fifteen restored moai, shows a monumental arrangement in an upright position. Hanga Poukura reveals another side of archaeological heritage: a low platform, stone fragments, and fallen statues. They are different sites and offer different experiences.

The southern coast also has [Ahu Akahanga](/chile/place/ahu-akahanga/), where traces of an early settlement and moai that have not been raised again remain. If a trip includes both unrestored sites, pay attention to the platforms' individual details and the guide's explanations so the stops do not become repeated photographs of similar ruins.

## How the excursion is organized

On programs featuring Hanga Poukura, the stop is part of a road excursion around the island. It does not require a separate multi-day outing. Rapa Nui itself, however, is far from mainland Chile and connected to Santiago by air. Check the order of island activities and especially flight times if Hanga Poukura is visited on departure day.

The archaeological site is in an open coastal landscape. Comfortable walking shoes are useful; climbing stone structures or sculptures is prohibited. Monuments should be viewed from permitted paths with a guide's explanations. Confirm access and the rules for protected areas before departure.

## Frequently asked questions about Hanga Poukura

### Can Hanga Poukura be visited on a short island tour?

Yes. The [three-day tour](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/) includes Hanga Poukura on day three, with Ahu Akivi, Puna Pau, and Tahai. An airport transfer follows.

### How does Hanga Poukura differ from Ahu Akivi?

At [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/), seven statues have been restored and stand on the platform. Hanga Poukura has fallen moai and the remains of a coastal complex. The difference between a restored and unrestored site is particularly clear on a combined excursion.

### Do all moai tours include Hanga Poukura?

No. Some itineraries visit other platforms only. Choose by the actual list of stops rather than a general promise to see Rapa Nui's moai.

## Ahu Nau Nau: an archaeological complex beside Anakena Beach

[Ahu Nau Nau](/chile/place/ahu-nau-nau/) is a ceremonial platform bearing moai statues near [Anakena Beach](/chile/place/anakena-beach/). Sand, ocean, and palms create one of Easter Island's most recognizable landscapes, but the site's significance extends far beyond beach photographs.

Restored sculptures stand on the platform. Some retain their red stone *pukao* headpieces. The figures' surfaces reveal details that are less visible on many other moai. Some of these features are thought to have survived because sand protected the stone for a period of time.

The ahu was a ceremonial structure associated with the ancestors of the local community. To understand Rapa Nui culture, it helps to regard the beach and monument as neighboring but distinct spaces.

## What to look for on the moai

Examine the contours of the faces, the position of the hands, and relief details on the backs of the sculptures. The pukao remind us that completing a moai involved several kinds of stonework.

The principal figures on many ahu were carved from volcanic tuff. Another type of stone, associated with [Puna Pau Quarry](/chile/place/puna-pau-quarry/), was used for the red headpieces. Pukao are often called stone "hats," but that is a modern simplification; researchers debate their precise symbolic meaning.

Compare Ahu Nau Nau with [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/), where seven figures stand inland, and [Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/), known for its long restored row. These sites occupy different landscapes and reveal the variety of island architecture.

## What archaeologists found in 1978

During the restoration of Ahu Nau Nau in **1978**, parts of a moai eye made from white coral with a red insert were discovered. Chile's Cultural Heritage Service and the Rapa Nui Museum describe this find.

It provided physical evidence that some statues may have had inset eyes. Researchers suggest these may have been installed after the moai were moved to the platform or during the final stages of preparation. The discovery changed our understanding of how the completed figures looked.

Surviving fragments and modern reconstructions are not the same thing. When bright eyes appear in photographs of other monuments, they should not automatically be assumed to be authentic ancient details. Ahu Nau Nau is particularly valuable because genuine archaeological evidence was found here.

## Combining an ahu visit with time by the sea

At [Anakena](/chile/place/anakena-beach/), you can make time both for the archaeological story and for walking along the sandy shore. Rapa Nui traditions connect the bay with the arrival of Hotu Matu'a, the island's legendary first ruler. This is part of traditional history and should be distinguished from a documented chronology.

For a meaningful sightseeing day, Ahu Nau Nau pairs well with [Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/), where statues were carved, and [Ahu Akahanga](/chile/place/ahu-akahanga/), where fallen moai remain. Together these tell the story of different stages in a monument's life: carving, erection, collapse, and modern excavation.

When choosing a [Chile tour](/chile/tour/), check whether time is allocated both to the platform and the shore. Simply mentioning Anakena in an itinerary does not reveal how thoroughly the moai will be explored.

## Protecting the monument and practical advice

Ahu Nau Nau is within the protected area of Rapa Nui National Park. For entry to archaeological sites, park authorities require a ticket and an accredited guide. Visitors must not cross barriers, climb the platform, touch statues, or collect stones.

If a day combines archaeology and beach time, pack closed shoes for the archaeological walks, sun protection, and beach essentials. Swimming depends on weather and sea conditions, while the excursion order follows access rules in force at the time.

## Frequently asked questions about Ahu Nau Nau

### Where is Ahu Nau Nau?

Near [Anakena Beach](/chile/place/anakena-beach/) on [Easter Island](/chile/place/easter-island/) in Chile.

### Why is the complex important to archaeology?

During excavations and restoration in **1978**, parts of a moai eye made from coral and red volcanic rock were found here. This helped explain how ancient statues were decorated.

### Can I see the statues and swim on the same day?

Yes, the platform is next to the beach. However, archaeological protection rules and conditions for swimming are separate matters.

### Which is more interesting, Ahu Nau Nau or Ahu Akivi?

They are different monuments. Ahu Nau Nau is known for its oceanfront setting and the discovery of moai eyes, while [Ahu Akivi](/chile/place/ahu-akivi/) features seven figures inland.

## Which itineraries include Ahu Nau Nau and Anakena Beach?

[Ahu Nau Nau](/chile/place/ahu-nau-nau/) is a ceremonial platform with moai statues beside [Anakena Beach](/chile/place/anakena-beach/) on Rapa Nui. It is a place where archaeology meets a sandy shore and palms. Some moai retain red stone headpieces, making the group particularly valuable for understanding what completed statues looked like.

Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} whose main programs stop at Ahu Nau Nau. When comparing trips, remember that the platform is usually seen together with Anakena after other archaeological areas. Total travel durations can differ substantially, and the amount of beach time depends on the specific day.

## A short island tour: archaeology in the morning and the coast later

On the [three-day Easter Island: moai and volcanoes journey](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/), day two follows the southern coast past [Ahu Akahanga](/chile/place/ahu-akahanga/) to [Rano Raraku Quarry](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/) and [Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/). Next come Te Pito Kura and Anakena, where Ahu Nau Nau stands. There is time for walking and swimming before the group returns to the hotel.

This format suits travelers who want to see different moai sites and end the day near the water. The three-day tour does not advertise a separate full beach day: this is a stop within a substantial excursion, not an independent beach holiday.

## What a mainland Chile program adds

On the [private ten-day tour](/chile/tour/chile-easter-island-private-tour-10-days/), Ahu Nau Nau is visited during the "Anakena" excursion. The route includes Ahu Akahanga, Rano Raraku, Tongariki, [Ahu Te Pito Kura](/chile/place/ahu-te-pito-kura/), and finishes at the beach. Other days include Santiago, Valparaíso, Viña del Mar, and archaeological sites elsewhere on Rapa Nui.

The [Colorful Santiago and Mysterious Easter Island tour](/chile/tour/santiago-easter-island/) also combines the Chilean capital with Anakena and the main platforms. The [12-day Best of Chile itinerary](/chile/tour/best-of-chile-easter-island-12-days/) adds the Atacama and Patagonia. Both suit travelers wanting to combine Polynesian culture with mainland Chilean nature, although fewer days are devoted to the island than might be spent on its beaches and archaeology alone.

## Ahu Nau Nau on multi-country journeys

On the [17-day Chile and Argentina itinerary](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-private-grand-tour-17-days/), Ahu Nau Nau is visited on a Rapa Nui history excursion including Rano Raraku, Tongariki, Te Pito Kura, and Anakena. After the island, the journey continues through other regions of Chile and Argentina, including Patagonia.

The [33-day Peru, Bolivia, and Chile program](/multi-country/tour/south-america-luxury-33-days/) also visits Ahu Nau Nau, but as part of a very different scale of travel. Here the island excursion is one stop in a long sequence of South American regions. If your main interest is the moai and island itself, a short standalone tour is simpler logistically.

## What you can compare in one sightseeing day

At [Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/), you see where moai were carved; [Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/) has fifteen restored upright figures; and [Te Pito Kura](/chile/place/ahu-te-pito-kura/) is known for a huge fallen statue. Ahu Nau Nau completes the sequence with a restored coastal complex beside a sandy beach. This route helps compare different stages of carving, installation, and preservation of moai.

When choosing a program, check whether free time for walking or swimming follows the visit to Ahu Nau Nau, and how meals are arranged on a long excursion day. For a true beach holiday, allocate additional time at Anakena separately from a packed archaeological itinerary.

## What to plan for the trip

Easter Island is linked to the mainland by flights via Santiago. When choosing a tour, check how many nights you actually spend on Rapa Nui and how visits to [Anakena](/chile/place/anakena-beach/) and other places are distributed. Wind and ocean conditions change along the coast; even with a beach stop scheduled, swimming depends on local weather and sea conditions.

Archaeological sites must be visited on authorized paths. Ahu Nau Nau's platform and statues are fragile heritage; climbing on structures and touching figures are prohibited.

## Frequently asked questions about tours to Ahu Nau Nau

### Are Ahu Nau Nau and Anakena Beach the same place?

They are neighboring places: Ahu Nau Nau is a [ceremonial platform with moai](/chile/place/ahu-nau-nau/), while [Anakena](/chile/place/anakena-beach/) is the beach. Itineraries usually visit them during one stop.

### Is swimming included at Ahu Nau Nau?

Several programs allow time for walking and swimming at Anakena, such as the [three-day island tour](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/). Actual access to the water depends on conditions on the visiting day.

### Is one excursion day enough for Ahu Nau Nau?

Yes, for seeing the platform as part of a tour of archaeological sites. If you want extended beach time, choose a program with additional hours at Anakena.

## Ahu Te Pito Kura: the giant Paro moai and Easter Island legends

Ahu Te Pito Kura is an archaeological site on the northern coast of [Easter Island](/chile/place/easter-island/), or Rapa Nui. Its main attraction is **the Paro moai**, one of the largest statues ever erected on an island ceremonial platform. Today the figure lies on the ground beside its ahu: its size and fallen position reveal a different aspect of moai history from restored sites.

Nearby is a rounded stone associated with local traditions and the name "Navel of the World." These two parts are best explored together while distinguishing archaeological facts from traditional beliefs. Paro is fascinating for the techniques used to carve and transport enormous statues; the stone is significant for the cultural meanings attached to it.

## Paro: why this moai stands out

Chile's Museum of Pre-Columbian Art describes Paro as about **10 meters** tall and approximately **85 tonnes** in weight. It is among the largest moai that were completed and placed on a platform rather than left in the quarry. The monument was carved from volcanic rock and then transported from its production site to the coast.

To appreciate the scale of that undertaking, first visit [Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/), where most moai were carved, and then Te Pito Kura. The quarry reveals the manufacturing process; this site shows the endpoint of the statue's ancient journey and the consequences of its fall.

Paro lies on the ground, making it especially interesting to imagine the figure standing upright with a guide's help. The platform, body proportions, and surviving fragments reveal the effort invested by the community that carved and moved it. Do not assume you can approach or touch the statue: the park establishes all visitor boundaries.

## The Te Pito o Te Henua stone and the "Navel of the World"

Near the ahu lies a large rounded stone associated with the concept of **Te Pito o Te Henua**. Tourist accounts often call it the "Navel of the World" and link it to legends about the arrival of the first settlers. This forms part of Rapa Nui cultural storytelling.

Visitors sometimes hear claims that the stone has special energy or unusual physical properties. **These should be understood as local beliefs and tourist stories, not established scientific facts.** The object has value as evidence of traditions and the islanders' relationship with their land.

View the stone and its surrounding barrier only from the permitted side. Climbing onto the stone, placing hands on it, or moving surrounding stones conflicts with archaeological conservation. Even a small object may be important to the site's historical context.

## How Te Pito Kura differs from Ahu Tongariki

Travelers often see both sites on the same day, but they reveal different chapters of the island's history.

| Site | What you see |
|---|---|
| [Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/) | 15 raised and restored moai |
| Te Pito Kura | The huge fallen Paro moai and a sacred stone |

[Ahu Vaihu](/chile/place/ahu-vaihu/) offers another comparison: an entire group of toppled statues lies on the ground there. Together these stops illustrate the difference between restored monuments and sites that preserve traces of destruction.

The story can conclude at [Anakena Beach](/chile/place/anakena-beach/) and nearby [Ahu Nau Nau](/chile/place/ahu-nau-nau/). Archaeology meets a sandy shore here; check whether the itinerary leaves enough actual time for a walk beside the ocean.

## Location and how to get there

Te Pito Kura is on the northeastern side of the island, near the coastal route toward Anakena. Most visitors stay and set off from [Hanga Roa](/chile/place/hanga-roa/), traveling by car with a guide.

Plan the day around roads and other stops rather than treating the site as a separate long trek. On a typical sightseeing route, visitors explore the southern coast and Rano Raraku, continue to Tongariki and Te Pito Kura, and finish at Anakena.

The stop itself generally takes less time than the complete island archaeology excursion. Its duration depends on the guide, your interest in the story, and the order of visits. For photographs of Paro, choose a viewpoint from which the entire statue is visible without leaving the authorized path.

## Tickets and mandatory guides in Rapa Nui National Park

Archaeological heritage sites are part of [Rapa Nui National Park](/chile/place/easter-island/), a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1995. The Ma'u Henua administration explicitly requires **an admission ticket and an accredited guide** for visiting park attractions.

Tickets can be obtained through the park's official service. At the time of the check, the park states that a ticket is valid for **10 consecutive days**. Certain particularly fragile sites, including Rano Raraku and Orongo, limit the number of visits permitted on one ticket. Account for these conditions when planning different days.

The rules also prohibit touching moai, crossing marked boundaries, taking stones, operating drones without permission, and commercial photography without prior approval. These are cultural-heritage protection requirements, not merely suggestions for a guide's convenience.

## Te Pito Kura on Ada Tours itineraries

On the [three-day Easter Island: moai and volcanoes tour](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/), Te Pito Kura is included on day two along with Ahu Vaihu, [Ahu Akahanga](/chile/place/ahu-akahanga/), Rano Raraku, Tongariki, and Anakena. This is a full-day private excursion with an English-speaking guide and a boxed lunch.

The [private ten-day Chile and Easter Island tour](/chile/tour/chile-easter-island-private-tour-10-days/) also includes a stop at Te Pito Kura after Tongariki in its island itinerary. It combines Rapa Nui sites with experiences on mainland Chile.

On [Colorful Santiago and Mysterious Easter Island](/chile/tour/santiago-easter-island/), the itinerary continues from Te Pito Kura to Anakena. This island excursion is in a group with an English-speaking guide. Compare the actual programs for format, meals, and transport: an identical archaeological stop does not mean the package of services is identical.

## Frequently asked questions about Ahu Te Pito Kura

### Why is the Paro moai lying down?

The statue was toppled and remains beside its ceremonial platform. The monuments' destruction is part of Rapa Nui's broader history, which guides discuss when visiting different ahu.

### Is Paro the tallest statue on Easter Island?

Paro is among the largest moai **completed and erected on an ahu**. Some unfinished figures in Rano Raraku Quarry may have been larger; those are a different category of monument.

### Is there proof of unusual energy at the "Navel of the World"?

Local legends link the stone to the islanders' spiritual traditions. This is cultural heritage, but claims of supernatural energy are not scientifically established properties of the stone.

### Is a guide required?

Yes. Rapa Nui National Park requires an accredited guide and valid ticket. These arrangements also apply if you plan the trip independently.

### What combines well with Te Pito Kura?

[Ahu Tongariki](/chile/place/ahu-tongariki/), [Rano Raraku](/chile/place/rano-raraku-volcano/), and [Anakena](/chile/place/anakena-beach/). This combination is included on the [three-day Ada Tours program](/chile/tour/easter-island-3-days/).
